lines.text: [excited] What if you could just... describe the app you need?
Every Jig app is a spec: screens, typed data, actions and schedules, written as JSON by Muse Spark.
The same spec runs natively on iPhone, Android and the web. There's no generated code to break.
Each change is checked against a JSON Schema built from the runtime itself, then every screen is rendered off-screen.
If anything fails, the errors go straight back to the model, and it repairs the app on its own.
One TypeScript runtime does the work everywhere: state, bindings, and a flexbox layout engine.
Each frame it sends a small batch of operations, and the native hosts draw real UIKit and Android views.
To change an app, select any element and say what you want, typed or spoken.
The model gets that element's exact place in the spec, patches only that, and checks a screenshot of the result.
The container gives every app storage, secrets, files, media and home-screen widgets.
A schedule in the spec becomes real OS notifications ahead of time, so reminders fire even when the app is closed.
Apps can publish lists to a personal data store on the device.
Another app can read them, live, once you allow it. Secrets never leave the app.
Apps can ask Muse Spark, find objects in photos with SAM 3.1, and get icons from Muse Image.
The shell makes those calls with your key, so apps never see it.
For parsing or file formats, the model can add a script. It runs sandboxed, with pinned libraries.
Even then, the interface stays a spec, drawn natively.
[playful] Here's one, start to finish.
One sentence describes the app.
Muse Spark builds it, and checks its own work.
[delighted] A real native app. On iPhone, and Android.
Plants and their schedules are stored on the device.
It'll even remind me while it's closed.
Want a change? Point at it, and say it.
It edits just that button, then checks a screenshot.
Due plants now stand out.
[warmly] Describe it. Use it. Change it. That's Jig.
